title: A bowl of stew (Genesis 25:19–34)
hookLine: Esau sells his birthright because he's hungry right now
carry: not for a bowl of stew

lines: SOLD FOR A BOWL OF STEW.
cards: You walk in starving after a long day. Someone's cooking, and the whole kitchen smells like onions and something slow-simmered. You'd say almost anything for a bowl.
Almost anything. Genesis has a story about exactly that moment. The Douay-Rheims calls the dish red pottage, and the Letter to the Hebrews calls it one mess: a single bowl of stew.
And the thing sold for it was a firstborn son's whole future.

teach.b: First, the twins. Rebecca, like Sarah before her, waits years for a child, and Isaac prays for her. When she conceives, the twins struggle so hard inside her that she asks God why.
God tells her: two nations are in your womb, and the elder will serve the younger. Esau is born first, red and hairy. Jacob comes out holding his brother's heel.
Esau grows into a hunter, a man of the open field; Jacob is a quiet man who stays among the tents. Isaac favors Esau; Rebecca favors Jacob. You can feel the trouble coming.
Second, the stew. One day Jacob is cooking lentils, and Esau comes in from the field, exhausted.
Give me some of that red stuff, he says. Jacob, quick as a trader, answers: sell me your birthright first. Third, the birthright.

teach.h: A DOUBLE SHARE AND A FUTURE.
teach.b: Later, the law in Deuteronomy gives the firstborn son a double share of all his father has. It was a future: the inheritance, and the family's name after the father.
And Esau says, I'm about to die, what good is a birthright to me? He swears it away, eats, drinks, gets up, and leaves. Fourth, the verdict.
Genesis doesn't lecture. It ends the scene with one line.
In the Douay-Rheims, Esau went his way, "making little account of having sold his first birthright."

teach.h: NOT FOR A BOWL OF STEW.
teach.b: The Letter to the Hebrews later remembers him as the man who traded his birthright for a single meal. Neither brother looks good here. Jacob drives a hard bargain with a hungry man.
But the story's eye is on what Esau threw away for right now.

how: Catholic tradition speaks of temperance, the virtue of moderating desires, and many Catholics practice small acts of self-denial, especially on Fridays and during Lent.

o: the firstborn's double share and future
a family's land, shared equally by all sons
the right to name a newborn child

games.q: what's inside the trade — tap the pairs.

s: Jacob tricks Esau into eating poisoned stew
it's ordinary lentil stew. Jacob simply asks for the birthright first, and Esau agrees.
in the Douay-Rheims, Esau's dish is called pottage
red pottage of lentils: a bowl of stew.
Genesis gives a long speech condemning Esau
it just says he went his way, making little account of what he'd sold.

games.q: you're Esau, home from the field, exhausted. your brother has stew on the fire and says: sell me your birthright first. what does the story say you do?
o: swear it away, eat, drink, and go.
games.why: what good is a birthright to me, he asks, and he swears it away, eats and leaves, "making little account of having sold his first birthright."

practice: Notice what you're craving right now, or what you usually reach for at this hour, a snack, a scroll, a quick look at your messages, and just name it without a fight.
Decide to wait until the bell rings, feel the pull of right now, the Esau pull, and notice whether you're still fine without it. If you pray, offer the waiting for something that matters more.

wordCard.voice: Birthright. The firstborn's double share and his place in the family's future. Esau sold his for a bowl of red lentil stew.

orig.note: Hebrew: birthright, the right of the firstborn. it sounds close to berakhah, blessing, tomorrow's story.

carryVoice: Your line: not for a bowl of stew. A whole future, for one hungry minute. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: making little account of having sold his first birthright.
